one_line_contribution: A generalizability-theory audit of self-editing agent memory that measures how much of a memory item's downstream utility is a stable item main effect versus item-by-query interaction, derives the probe budget the per-item assumption implies, and tests whether an item-level prune decision beats removing the same number of items at random on held-out episodes.
closest_prior_work: The proposal names MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) as the closest work and correctly distinguishes it, but that is the wrong neighborhood. The real threat is the data-valuation literature the proposal barely touches: the point-removal benchmarking line (OpenDataVal, Data Banzhaf, and the Kwon/Jia-adjacent evaluations) has repeatedly shown that per-instance value scores are unstable across resampling and that removal by score frequently fails to beat random removal — which is P-1, P-2 and P-4 in a different substrate. The proposal cites only arXiv:2406.04606 from this cluster and dismisses it as 'fine-tuning data, no probe-budget derivation'; a reviewer who knows the valuation literature will read the contribution as a domain transplant with a G-theory wrapper. Second threat: the ICL demonstration-instability line (Lu et al. 2022 on order sensitivity; work showing demonstration utility is query-conditional). Memory items injected into context are demonstrations, so 'item x query interaction dominates the item main effect' is qualitatively pre-established there. Novelty then rests on the quantitative probe-budget derivation and the CI-gated prune rule, which is a thinner contribution than the abstract implies.
strongest_objection: The two headline numbers are close to guaranteed by the chosen budget rather than by the phenomenon, so the audit cannot separate 'item value is unstable' from 'this study lacks resolution.' (a) P-3 — 'fewer than 10% of items have a 95% CI excluding zero' — is stated as the sharpest number in the paper, but Measurement and Noise Control concedes the per-item detectable effect at ~85 binary observations is ~±20 accuracy points. No one, including the curation papers under attack, believes a single item in a 120-item bank moves episode accuracy by 20 points. So P-3 is an arithmetic consequence of choosing 85 observations per item; it would come out the same in a world where every item had a perfectly stable +3-point effect. (b) P-4 — 'P1 - P2 within ±4 points, CI covering zero' — sets an equivalence band that is plausibly wider than the entire memory effect in this setup. The precheck gates only on ≥8% instance-level *disagreement* (churn), not on any net effect, and the track's own prior result is that a full bank fixed zero and broke six or seven items, i.e. a net effect of roughly a point. Removing 12 of 120 items cannot move an 800-instance paired comparison by 4 points under any hypothesis about item value, so the predicted null arrives regardless of whether the curation literature's premise is true. P3 does not rescue this: it is a transfer ceiling estimated on the same mismatched probe distribution, not an in-sample bound on how much *any* 12-item prune could move the metric. A second, independent version of the same problem: the item x query variance component is what P-1 hinges on, and the proposal never states how many distinct probe instances the 3,000 episodes cover. With 120 items and ~10,500 item-appearances, if the probe set is a few hundred instances then almost every (item, query) cell has zero or one binary observation, and item x query variance is not separably identified from Bernoulli residual — the 600-episode second-seed replicate only re-runs whole episodes and does not fix cell-level identification for the other 2,400. A headline decomposition whose largest component may be unidentified is not a decomposition.
what_would_fix_it: Three concrete changes, in order of importance. (1) Add an in-sample detectability ceiling: fit item effects on the held-out test set itself and prune the 12 worst, reported as an oracle arm. If even the test-fitted prune moves under 4 points, the paper has shown its outcome measure cannot resolve any 12-item decision, and the honest finding becomes a measurement-resolution result rather than a claim about item value — still publishable, but a different paper. If it moves well above 4 points while P1 does not, the transfer claim becomes real and decisive. (2) Report the total headroom the ±4-point band is being judged against: a no-memory arm and a full-bank arm on the same 800 paired instances, with the net delta and the fix/break decomposition. Equivalence bands must be calibrated to the phenomenon, not to the sample size. (3) Re-express P-3 relative to what is achievable: report the fraction of items whose CI excludes zero alongside the fraction that *could* exclude zero under a plausible true-effect distribution (e.g. simulate items with stable effects of 2, 5, 10 points at the same budget). Additionally, state the probe-set instance count and the expected observations per (item, query) cell, and either add cell-level replication or drop the item x query component in favour of a directly estimable stable-versus-total ratio. Finally, either align the probe injection distribution with deployment top-k (probe by swapping one retrieved item for its rank-k+1 successor, which is the actual prune counterfactual) or reframe the estimand explicitly as marginal-over-random-subsets and stop calling P1 vs P2 decisive.
missing_baseline: Two. First, an in-sample/oracle prune fitted on the held-out test set itself (distinct from P3, which is fitted on the full probe set and inherits the same distribution mismatch) — without it, a null on P1 vs P2 is indistinguishable from the metric having no resolution at the 12-item scale, and the paper's own Risk 4 cannot be discharged. Second, an empty-bank / no-memory arm in Phase 3. Given the track's prior finding that memory was net harmful, the practically relevant comparator is 'turn memory off', and P9 (tune k on a dev split) may simply select k=0, in which case the constructive corollary 'budget control dominates curation' silently reduces to 'do not use memory' — a very different recommendation that the current condition set cannot distinguish or report.
preprint_collision: The check is unusually honest about process — it states 14 queries, a single pass, a blocked second round, and names the specific scenario (a random-removal ablation buried in a curation preprint) that would gut the headline. That candour is worth credit. But it searched the wrong neighbourhood thoroughly and the right one not at all. Every cluster swept is agent-memory-side (A-MAC, SAGE, MEMAUDIT, GovMem, EDV, Memory-R1, A-MEM, PlugMem); the two literatures that actually threaten the claim are absent. (i) Data-valuation benchmarking, where 'per-instance scores are unstable under resampling' and 'value-ranked removal does not beat random removal' are established results with published point-removal protocols — the proposal touches this cluster with one citation (arXiv:2406.04606) and waves it off on substrate grounds, which is precisely the move a reviewer will refuse. (ii) ICL demonstration sensitivity, which already establishes qualitatively that demonstration utility is query-conditional rather than a property of the demonstration. Neither absence is a hard collision — I can name no preprint that runs this exact variance decomposition on an agent memory bank — but a novelty claim resting on a single-pass search that never queried the field where the same negative result is textbook is not established novelty. The residual-risk paragraph should be extended to cover these clusters, and the related work should argue the transplant is non-obvious rather than pretending the source result does not exist.
